results.name: late_minus_early_yes_rate
results.description: Yes rate on trials with trial_index >= 225 minus yes rate on trials < 225; observed below null means people say yes less as the session goes on, a drift the stationary model does not produce.

results.name: target_in_set_yes_rate
results.description: Yes rate when the target is one of the shown examples (0.5 if no such trials); observed below null means people reject already-seen examples more than the model (which says near-certain yes) predicts.

results.name: between_set_yes_rate_variance
results.description: Variance across example sets (with >=10 trials) of the per-set yes rate; observed above null means people's generalisation breadth differs between sets more sharply than the model predicts (observed below null: the model makes sets too different).

results.name: single_example_yes_rate
results.description: Yes rate on trials whose set has exactly one example, excluding target equal to the example (0.5 if none); observed above/below null means the model under/over-generalises from a single example.
results.code:
# name: single_example_yes_rate
# description: Yes rate on trials whose set has exactly one example, excluding target equal to the example (0.5 if none); observed above/below null means the model under/over-generalises from a single example.
def test_statistic(df):
    s = df["number_set"].astype(str)
    one = (s.str.count(",") == 0).to_numpy()
    ex1 = pd.to_numeric(s.str.split(",").str[0], errors="coerce").to_numpy()
    tgt = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy()
    m = one & (ex1 != tgt)
    if m.sum() == 0:
        return 0.5
    return float(df["rating"].to_numpy()[m].mean())

results.name: shared_last_digit_target_yes_rate
results.description: Among sets of >=2 examples that all share a last digit, the yes rate for non-example targets with that same last digit (0.5 if none); observed above/below null means the model under/over-generalises the "ends in d" rule.
results.code:
# name: shared_last_digit_target_yes_rate
# description: Among sets of >=2 examples that all share a last digit, the yes rate for non-example targets with that same last digit (0.5 if none); observed above/below null means the model under/over-generalises the "ends in d" rule.
def test_statistic(df):
    ex = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce")
    n = ex.notna().sum(axis=1).to_numpy()
    last = (ex % 10).to_numpy()
    first = last[:, 0]
    same = np.all((last == first[:, None]) | np.isnan(last), axis=1) & (n >= 2)
    tgt = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy()
    in_set = (ex.to_numpy() == tgt[:, None]).any(axis=1)
    m = same & (tgt % 10 == first) & ~in_set
    if m.sum() == 0:
        return 0.5
    return float(df["rating"].to_numpy()[m].mean())

results.name: sequential_yes_dependence
results.description: P(yes | previous trial yes) minus P(yes | previous trial no), over consecutive trials (trial_index increments by 1 in row order); observed above null means response perseveration/autocorrelation the trial-independent model lacks.

results.name: magnitude_proximity_gradient
results.description: For non-example targets, yes rate when the target is within 5 of the nearest example minus yes rate when it is more than 20 from every example; observed above null means people generalise by numeric closeness more strongly than the model's interval hypotheses allow.
results.code:
# name: magnitude_proximity_gradient
# description: For non-example targets, yes rate when the target is within 5 of the nearest example minus yes rate when it is more than 20 from every example; observed above null means people generalise by numeric closeness more strongly than the model's interval hypotheses allow.
def test_statistic(df):
    ex = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy()
    tgt = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy()
    d = np.nanmin(np.abs(ex - tgt[:, None]), axis=1)
    r = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    near = (d > 0) & (d <= 5)
    far = d > 20
    if near.sum() == 0 or far.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(r[near].mean() - r[far].mean())

results.name: parity_match_effect
results.description: Among sets of >=2 examples that are all odd or all even, yes rate for non-example same-parity targets minus opposite-parity targets; observed above null means people use parity more than the model, below null means the model over-relies on odd/even.
results.code:
# name: parity_match_effect
# description: Among sets of >=2 examples that are all odd or all even, yes rate for non-example same-parity targets minus opposite-parity targets; observed above null means people use parity more than the model, below null means the model over-relies on odd/even.
def test_statistic(df):
    ex = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy()
    n = (~np.isnan(ex)).sum(axis=1)
    par = ex % 2
    p0 = par[:, 0]
    same = np.all((par == p0[:, None]) | np.isnan(par), axis=1) & (n >= 2)
    tgt = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy()
    in_set = (ex == tgt[:, None]).any(axis=1)
    r = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    match = same & ~in_set & ((tgt % 2) == p0)
    mis = same & ~in_set & ((tgt % 2) != p0)
    if match.sum() == 0 or mis.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(r[match].mean() - r[mis].mean())
